flashcards.q: Why does BFS guarantee that the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest path, in an unweighted graph?
flashcards.a: BFS exhausts every path of length k before considering any path of length k+1, since it processes the queue in strict FIFO order layer by layer. No path discovered later (at a greater layer) can be shorter than one discovered earlier.

flashcards.q: What is the single most damaging implementation bug in BFS, and what does it cause?
flashcards.a: Marking a node visited at DEQUEUE time instead of ENQUEUE time. This allows the same node to be pushed onto the queue multiple times via different paths before it's ever processed, degrading complexity past O(V+E) toward O(V*E) in dense graphs.

flashcards.q: What line of code turns plain BFS into level-aware BFS, and why is it necessary?
flashcards.a: level_size = len(queue), captured BEFORE draining the current level's nodes. Without this snapshot, there's no way to tell where one level ends and the next begins in a single flat FIFO queue.

flashcards.q: For a 'nearest occurrence of X' problem like Walls and Gates or Rotting Oranges, why seed the queue with ALL sources simultaneously rather than looping single-source BFS per source?
flashcards.a: Seeding all sources at distance 0 together computes true minimum distances in one O(V+E) pass. Looping single-source BFS once per source is also correct but costs O(k*(V+E)) for k sources -- a real complexity difference interviewers specifically probe for.

flashcards.q: Why is DFS the wrong default tool for a shortest-path or minimum-steps question, even though it's also O(V+E)?
flashcards.a: DFS finds A path on first discovery of a node, with no guarantee it's the shortest. Using DFS correctly for shortest path requires exploring all paths and comparing afterward, which costs more and is more code than just using BFS, which guarantees shortest-by-construction.

flashcards.q: What is 0-1 BFS, and when should you reach for it instead of plain BFS or Dijkstra?
flashcards.a: 0-1 BFS uses a deque instead of a plain queue: push a neighbor to the FRONT when relaxed via a 0-weight edge, to the BACK when relaxed via a 1-weight edge. Use it when all edge weights are restricted to {0,1} -- it recovers Dijkstra-correct shortest distances in O(V+E) instead of Dijkstra's O((V+E) log V).

flashcards.q: Why does bidirectional BFS reduce the search space from O(b^d) to roughly O(2*b^(d/2))?
flashcards.a: Growing frontiers simultaneously from both the start and the (known) target means each frontier only needs to expand to the halfway depth (d/2) before they meet, rather than one frontier expanding the full depth d alone.

flashcards.q: In Word Ladder, why is generating neighbors by scanning the entire dictionary per word inefficient, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Scanning the whole dictionary per word costs O(N*L) per word. The fix is generating all 26*L single-character substitutions of the current word and checking dictionary membership directly (O(26*L) per word), or precomputing wildcard-pattern buckets like 'h*t' -> {hot, hat, ...}.

flashcards.q: Why can plain BFS not be used directly on a graph with non-uniform edge weights?
flashcards.a: BFS's FIFO queue treats every edge as costing exactly one step, so it can't distinguish a cheap edge from an expensive one. If weights vary, the first-discovery path BFS finds may not actually be the lowest-total-weight path -- Dijkstra (or 0-1 BFS for the {0,1} special case) is needed instead.

flashcards.q: In Word Ladder II, why can't you simply mark a word visited the instant it's first discovered, the way the length-only version does?
flashcards.a: Word Ladder II needs to recover ALL shortest transformation sequences, and multiple words at the same BFS layer might transform into the same word at the next layer -- each is a valid parent for a shortest path. Marking visited immediately mid-layer would suppress some of those valid parents and lose valid shortest paths.
